paper_title: $π^4$: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: $π^4$ is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild---a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence---it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, $π^4$ achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation. With a shared backbone, the full geometry-and-motion system contains approximately 0.5B parameters---less than half the size of most baselines. It produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass, including large-scale scenes with thousands of input images despite training with contexts of at most 64 views. We further present the data and training recipe underlying these capabilities, together with empirical studies of key design choices. Code and models are available at https://github.com/yyfz/Pi4.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Feed-forward models have established powerful paradigm for reconstructing scenes directly from RGB observations [1, 2, 3]. More recently, this paradigm has been extended beyond scene reconstruction to encompass motion recovery [4, 5]. key question, however, is how well these capabilities generalize to in-the-wild observations, where scene content, camera configurations, temporal continuity, and the number of observations are unconstrained. Maintaining high-quality geometric reconstruction while robustly recovering motion from such diverse inputs remains significant practical challenge. To address this challenge, we present π4, unified foundation model for 4D scene perception from RGB observations. It handles single images, unordered image collections, and videos, recovering dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D and 3D point tracks and movingobject masks for multi-image inputs. Across the geometry benchmarks in Table 2, π4 achieves the best overall average rank among the compared methods, while delivering competitive performance in singleand multiview 2D/3D tracking and moving-object segmentation (Figure 2). Despite this broad functionality, the model employs shared backbone across these capabilities and contains approximately 0.5B parameters in totalless than half the size of most baselines. Beyond benchmark results, Figure 1 showcases joint geometry and motion reconstruction across diverse in-thewild observations, including aerial footage, casual handheld recordings, driving and sports scenes, and stylized content. These reconstruction and tracking results are all produced in single forward pass per scene. This combination of accuracy, efficiency, and generality is enabled by coordinated choices in model architecture, training, and data. At the architectural level, the geometry network of π4 retains the permutation-equivariant formulation of π3 [3], treating all input views symmetrically without designating reference view. Both the geometry and motion branches employ looped Transformer decoding [6], which we adopt for its strong cross-benchmark performance and parameter efficiency. We choose loop weight sharing partly to reduce memory usage, freeing capacity for larger within-sequence contexts. Training stochastically samples view counts from single images, 224-view sets, and 32/48/64-view sets, with short contexts dominating the mixture. sparse 3D refiner [7] further enhances local surface structure and geometric detail. To incorporate motion estimation without compromising reconstruction, we freeze the geometry network and train separate geometry-conditioned motion decoder. Direct 3D tracking couples correspondence estimation with geometry, camera placement, and scene scale in the regression 2 target. We instead keep motion prediction in image space and delegate 3D reasoning to the reconstruction branch, composing the two analytically. This yields simple correspondence objective that is independent of scene scale, while placing every visible 3D track point on the reconstructed target-view surface. Geometry features also provide useful context for correspondence prediction. Complementing these architectural and modeling choices, our data construction pipeline addresses gaps in scene and camera coverage, as well as the difficulty of obtaining geometric supervision for foregrounddominated videos. We render scene-level assets from Funes [8] and Sketchfab [9], covering architectural environments and other large-scale scenes rather than isolated objects alone. Coverage-aware view selection and connected view sampling balance broad scene coverage with local cross-view matchability, while complementary natural and counterbias camera configurations expand the range of roll angles and focal lengths encountered during training. We further apply field-of-view and lens augmentation to diversify image-to-ray mappings beyond those induced by conventional pinhole or rectified imagery. For Internet videos dominated by moving foregrounds, we infer background geometry following foreground suppression and video inpainting. We retain only points corresponding to originally visible background pixels and pair the resulting pseudo-labels with the original RGB frames. GameRealm [10], developed jointly with collaborators, further provides complementary engine-native geometry and persistent point trajectories as supervision for dynamic scenes. Together, these architectural, data, and training choices enable coherent joint reconstruction and tracking from thousands of images in large-scale scenes despite maximum training context of 64 views (Figure 1). We further examine the architecture and training strategy of π4 through targeted ablations and qualitative comparisons, highlighting the empirical findings and practical trade-offs that motivate these choices.

sections.title: 2.1 Visual Geometry Reconstruction
sections.content: Classical structure-from-motion (SfM) estimates cameras and sparse structure through image matching and bundle adjustment, while multi-view stereo (MVS) reconstructs dense surfaces from calibrated views. COLMAP exemplifies this modular pipeline [11, 12]. Learned MVS methods such as MVSNet [13] learn cost-volume regularization while retaining camera calibration as input. More recently, DUSt3R [1] predicts pairwise pointmaps without supplied cameras, and MASt3R [14] combines this 3D representation with learned matching descriptors, bridging reconstruction and correspondence estimation. Feed-forward multi-view models increasingly estimate geometry and cameras jointly. VGGT [2] predicts cameras, depth, pointmaps, and tracks from image sets, while π3 and its released Pi3X variant [3] use permutation-equivariant modeling without privileged input reference. MapAnything [15] targets metric reconstruction with flexible geometric inputs, whereas Depth Anything 3 3 [16] uses depth and ray prediction across arbitrary views. VGGT-Ω [17] incorporates matching supervision, and DVLT [6] reuses Transformer blocks through looped decoding. Monocular models provide complementary components: MoGe2 [18] separates metric-scale prediction from relative geometry, and MoGe3 [7] refines surface detail with sparse volumetric processing. Together, these methods provide complementary designs for joint camerageometry estimation, reference-free reconstruction, metric prediction, and iterative decoding. 2.

sections.title: Image Correspondence and Point Tracking
sections.content: Classical image tracking estimates motion through local appearance alignment, as in Lucas Kanade [19]. Modern optical-flow models such as RAFT [20] learn dense two-frame correspondence, while TAPIR [21] and CoTracker3 [22] follow queried points over videos and estimate visibility. CoWTracker [23] replaces correlation-volume lookup with iterative feature warping. Optical flow and query-based tracking thus provide dense or sparse image-space correspondences, typically within ordered video sequences.

sections.title: 2.3 Dynamic Scene Reconstruction and 4D Perception
sections.content: Dynamic scene reconstruction extends geometry estimation to scenes with moving and deforming content. Shape of Motion [24] reconstructs 4D scenes from monocular videos using compact SE(3) motion bases and data-driven geometric and tracking priors. MonST3R [25] instead adapts pointmap reconstruction to dynamic videos by estimating per-timestep geometry without an explicit motion representation. These approaches connect scene geometry with temporal variation, but differ in how motion is represented and how reconstruction and tracking are coupled. Recent methods further extend tracking to 3D and connect it to scene reconstruction. D4RT [26] and ARROW [5] use query-based decoding to recover point positions across time and reference cameras; ARROW additionally supports unordered and multiview observations. MoSE3 [27] models dense world-space motion through per-pixel SE(3) transformations, while Track4World [4] combines dense correspondences, geometry, and camera estimation for world-centric tracking. Moving-object segmentation provides complementary object-level characterization of scene dynamics by identifying regions that undergo motion [28, 29]. Across these directions, methods differ in their supported input configurations, output representations, and the degree to which geometry and motion are modeled jointly.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: π4 combines geometric reconstruction and motion estimation within single feed-forward model (Figure 3). shared image encoder provides features to two task-specific looped Transformer decoders. The geometry branch predicts dense pointmaps, camera poses, and metric scale; sparse 3D refiner then improves the predicted pointmaps. Conditioned on geometry features, the motion branch predicts image-space point tracks and moving-object masks. The predicted tracks are lifted to 3D using the reconstructed target-view geometry.

sections.title: 4.1 Data Sources and Mixture
sections.content: We combine public datasets with scene-level synthetic renderings, curated Internet videos, and game-based supervision to broaden scene and camera coverage and provide complementary supervision for dynamic scenes. Motion training uses point trajectories, static geometric correspondences, and real-video masks. Table 1 summarizes the data sources and sampling probabilities in the final geometry and motion training stages.

sections.title: 4.2 Scene-Level Synthetic Data
sections.content: Scene assets. We curate approximately 10,000 scene-level 3D assets from Funes [8] and Sketchfab [9] for synthetic multi-view rendering. These assets include architectural environments and other large-scale scenes, rather than only isolated objects. They support exterior observations and, where the geometry permits, interior views. Our goal is to broaden the diversity of scene layouts and camera configurations represented during training, rather than simply increase the number of rendered images. Candidate views and validation. We generate candidate cameras across positions, elevations, viewing directions, and distances using surrounding-space and surface-guided proposals. Exterior views capture both overall structure and local detail; interior views require sufficient free space and renderable surfaces. Visibility and RGB-D quality checks reject invalid cameras and degenerate observations, including views dominated by open mesh backsides. Coverage-aware views and connected chains. sections.title: 4.3 Sequence-Consistent Projection Augmentation
sections.content: Geometry training data are dominated by pinhole or rectified imagery, limiting the camera projections encountered during training. To counter this bias, we apply sequence-consistent lens and crop-and-resize augmentation. Each sequence receives an identity, barrel, blended equidistant (fisheye-like), or pincushion mapping with probability 40%, 35%, 20%, or 5%, respectively. Lens parameters and the final crop and resize are shared across frames. The augmentation transforms RGB and prepared geometric supervision together. For each output pixel, an inverse warp identifies source location whose calibrated ray and camera-axis depth define the new point target, without approximating the distorted view with new pinhole camera. Correspondence targets, visibility, and cross-view overlap are recomputed under the same mapping, while camera poses and scene scale remain unchanged. We crop to valid source-image support and resize, reducing distortion strength when necessary to satisfy zoom limit. These transforms diversify image-to-ray mappings within the observed field of view, complementing genuine camera diversity.

sections.title: 4.4 Foreground-Suppressed Supervision from Internet Videos
sections.content: Foreground-dominated reconstruction failures. Large moving foregrounds in Internet videos can disrupt geometry reconstruction, especially in egocentric sequences where the foreground dominates the view. These failures motivate suppressing the foreground and completing the video before geometry inference. Foreground-suppressed pseudo-labeling. We first mask moving foreground regions and complete the video using generative video inpainting [84, 85]. An earlier geometry-only checkpoint of π4 then infers background reconstruction from the completed video. We filter the resulting point clouds using the moving-object masks Figure 5: Internet-video data pipeline. Background geometry is reconstructed and filtered with moving-object masks. 10 and retain only points corresponding to originally visible background pixels. This avoids placing pseudo-labels directly on inpainted content. We pair these pseudo-labels with the original RGB frames, rather than the completed video, for subsequent geometry training. Figure 5 summarizes this pipeline.

sections.title: 4.5 GameRealm: Game-Based Geometry and Motion
sections.content: To broaden supervision for joint geometry and motion learning in dynamic environments, we use GameRealm [10], game-based dataset developed jointly with collaborators. It provides enginenative geometric and motion annotations, including posed multi-view RGB-D observations for reconstruction and persistent 2D/3D point trajectories for tracking. Covering diverse scenes, viewpoints, characters, and interactions, these data complement our static scene renderings and realvideo pseudo-labels with supervision for both spatial reconstruction and temporal correspondence.

sections.title: 4.6 Training Protocol
sections.content: π4 is trained progressively on 64 NVIDIA A800 GPUs, with approximately 300,000 optimizer updates across geometry-training stages. Starting from pretrained DINOv3 encoder, early stages train the image encoder, looped decoder, and point, camera, and matching heads. Later stages introduce sparse 3D refinement and metric-scale estimation while expanding the data mixture with curated Internet videos. Successive stages inherit the preceding model weights. Separately, motion training spans approximately 100,000 updates, including joint optimization of the motion decoder, tracking head, and moving-object mask head, with geometry frozen throughout. The SAM image encoder remains frozen during mask training, and the confidence head is trained separately with geometry fixed. Optimization uses AdamW and BF16 mixed precision. In the final geometry stage, images have long side of 512 pixels and varying aspect ratios, with at most 64 images per GPU and no gradient accumulation. For sets of views (Section 6.2), each GPU packs 64/K independent examples per batch. The base and encoder learning rates are 1.5 105 and 2 106, respectively, with cosine decay. All update counts denote optimizer steps under weighted data sampling, rather than dataset epochs.

sections.title: 5.1 Geometry Evaluation
sections.content: Standard benchmarks. Table 2 compares π4 with nine baselines across 16 settings spanning depth [86, 87, 88, 89], pose and trajectory [90, 74, 91, 38], and multiview reconstruction [92, 93, 94, 95]. Monocular depth uses per-frame median-scale alignment, whereas video depth uses sequencelevel scale-and-shift alignment. The full geometry-and-motion system has approximately 0.5B parameters, including frozen modules; Table 2 instead reports 343M loaded parameters for the geometry model used in this comparison. π4 achieves the best overall average rank (3.00, compared with 3.10 for Pi3X), with the best panelaverage ranks for video depth, pose/trajectory, and multiview reconstruction. sections.content: Figures 1, 6, and 7 show reconstructed geometry and motion across scenes and visual styles. Figure 7 illustrates the geometric consistency of the lifted tracks. In the 64-frame example (second row), ARROWs trajectories at later frames with cameras farther from the first-frame origin deviate visibly from the geometry reconstructed for the corresponding frames, whereas our lifted trajectories remain registered with the reconstructed surfaces. This observation is consistent with the error coupling that arises when independently regressed 3D endpoints are composed with camera estimates in first-frame reference system. sections.title: 6 Design Choices and Empirical Observations
sections.content: We study the architectural and training choices underlying π4 through targeted ablations and qualitative comparisons, highlighting the empirical findings and practical trade-offs that inform our final design. For loss-based ablations, we use matched model-development configurations, and percentage changes refer to relative differences in validation loss unless otherwise stated.

sections.title: 6.1 Looped Transformers: Training Dynamics and Step Conditioning
sections.content: Following DVLT [6], we use looped Transformer decoder with explicit loop-step conditioning. The looped and non-looped reconstruction models follow similar early training trajectories, but the looped models advantage emerges later in training and is more pronounced with step conditioning. Figure 8 shows the training and validation objectives of these decoder variants. separate comparison within the looped architecture isolates the effect of conditioning: adding the step signal reduces local point loss by 2.8% and camera loss by 10.2% relative to the unconditioned baseline. These results support the use of step conditioning in our decoder. 15 Figure 8: Training dynamics of looped decoders. The iteration-conditioned looped decoder achieves lower training and validation objectives than the non-looped baseline later in training.

sections.title: 6.2 Training View Counts and Memory Allocation
sections.content: We allocate part of the training memory budget to larger joint-view contexts, rather than using it only to pack more independent short examples. Our training recipe spans single-image inputs, short view sets of 224 images, and long view sets of 32, 48, or 64 images. View counts are sampled stochastically: short view sets receive most of the probability mass, with additional mass assigned to single-image inputs and the long-view buckets. This mixture combines frequent smallcontext updates with regular exposure to larger sets of observations. Figure 9: Training memory. Peak allocated memory per full update on an A800 80GB GPU: 512 512 inputs, BF16, 16 loop steps, and activation recomputation. The view count refers to images from one scene or sequence, not the aggregate image count across independent examples in batch. Including larger view sets gives the model direct training exposure to combining evidence across many observations, rather than relying exclusively on extrapolation from short inputs. This training choice complements weight sharing in the looped architecture. Figure 9 reports the measured training-memory footprint for input sets up to 64 views.

sections.title: 6.3 Encoder Layer Selection and Fine-Tuning
sections.content: Layer selection. UFM [102, Appendix E] shows that intermediate features from frozen encoder can outperform its final-layer features for dense prediction. Our geometry ablations using DINOv3 [30] show consistent trend. Jointly using layers 11 and 17 gives the best local point reconstruction and camera estimation among the combinations evaluated. This pair, also used in RoMa v2 [103], supplies the input to our multi-view decoder. Freezing and learning rate. Fine-tuning the encoder at 104 initially reduces the loss faster than freezing the encoder, but performs worse later in training. By contrast, fine-tuning at 105 reduces local point loss by 8.1% and camera loss by 4.5% relative to freezing. The comparison therefore depends on both learning rate and training duration. Our encoder remains trainable, with lower learning rate than the decoder and prediction heads.

sections.title: 6.4 Output Factorization and Geometric Consistency
sections.content: Local geometry and camera placement. Following π3 [3], we predict camera-local pointmaps and camera poses rather than directly regressing global pointmap. Global point errors mix errors in 16 local surface geometry with errors in its cross-view placement. Image evidence may constrain local surface structure even when the relative camera configuration remains uncertain. Separate localpoint and camera supervision preserves this distinction, allowing local geometry to be learned without requiring global placement to be equally accurate. Correspondence and 3D tracking. Factorizing 3D tracking into image-space correspondence prediction and geometric lifting avoids asking the motion head to independently reproduce targetview geometry and camera placement when predicting 3D endpoints or displacements. For visible tracks, lifting enforces agreement with the target geometry at the predicted correspondence by construction; independently predicted 3D positions need not satisfy this constraint. Figure 10 compares each methods native 3D tracks with its own reconstruction. In the global views, ARROWs directly regressed reference-frame endpoints degrade as target cameras move farther from the query view and the scene extent grows; late trajectories drift far from the corresponding scene structure. MoSE3 and π4 produce similarly coherent global trajectories, consistent with the numerical benefit of regressing image-space coordinates rather than large reference-frame XYZ values. The local close-ups reveal different source of error. MoSE3 lifts its UV predictions using an independently predicted tracking depth, which can place track off the reconstructed surface even when its global trajectory looks plausible. π4 instead samples target-view geometry at the predicted correspondence, without separate XYZ or tracking-depth prediction. Visible endpoints therefore lie on the reconstructed surface by construction, removing this independent source of trackgeometry disagreement. Figure 10: Motion parameterization. Top: local trackgeometry close-ups; bottom: global tracks. ARROW regresses XYZ, MoSE3 predicts UV and depth, and π4 lifts UV through geometry. Independent depth can separate MoSE3 tracks from reconstructed surfaces; ours remain registered by construction.

sections.title: 6.5 Geometry-Conditioned Motion
sections.content: Our geometry-conditioned motion branch is designed to reuse the spatial correspondence cues integrated by the geometry branch across views. Rather than independently learning cross-view spatial relationships, the motion branch conditions on this representation through Spatial AdaLN. In our ablation, geometry-feature conditioning reduces EPE by 7.17 px overall and 8.10 px on large-camera-baseline pairs compared with an otherwise identical model without this conditioning. These improvements show that geometry features provide useful spatial context for motion estimation, particularly for image pairs with large camera baselines.

sections.title: 6.6 Camera Supervision and Gradient Routing
sections.content: Camera targets. Our camera ablations favor the reference-free formulation of π3 with relative pose supervision [3] over regression tied to an explicitly designated reference frame, with more efficient convergence. We therefore use relative pose supervision, together with patch-matching supervision [17] to support learning at initialization, when relative-pose optimization is difficult [3, Appendix A.4]. Camera readout. In an early parameter-matched comparison, patch-token readout gives lower local point and camera losses than readout from dedicated register token. We therefore retain patch-token readout for the camera decoder. 17 Normalization gradients. Camera translation shares the predicted local-point normalization defined in Section 3.5. In that sections notation, s(P) is the sequence-wide mean valid norm of predicted local points, distinct from the subsequently fitted alignment scale a. We normalize the points while stopping the gradient through this same s(P) on the camera-translation path: (cid:101)P = s(P) , (cid:101)t = sg(s(P)) . (11) This preserves the shared normalization in the forward pass but prevents the camera objective from changing the point normalization through this gradient path. The local-point objective still differentiates through s(P). The operation neither detaches the camera prediction nor removes interactions between tasks through their shared representation. In the normalization ablation, detaching this gradient path reduces camera loss by 10.9%, while local point loss remains nearly unchanged, with 0.2% increase. Our camera objective uses this gradient-routing choice.

sections.title: 6.7 Relative-Point Supervision and Loss Weighting
sections.content: Supervising geometry constructed from multiple predicted quantities is established practice: VGGT-Ω [17] forms point maps from depth and camera predictions, while DA3 [16] supervises points constructed from depth and rays. We use relative-point supervision alongside local-point and camera objectives. In the loss-weight ablation, increasing the relative-point weight by an order of magnitude reduces local point loss by 5.4% and camera loss by 2.3%. Removing this term and compensating with stronger local-point objective does not recover the same camera quality; further increasing the local-point weight does not consistently help. These comparisons guide the loss weighting in our model.

sections.title: 6.8 Dense Prediction Heads: Practical Trade-offs
sections.content: Motivated by PXDepths monocular-depth results, we tested PXDepth/PixelDiT-inspired pixellevel head [104, 105] in place of the standard convolutional head. Patch-aligned artifacts persisted in local point predictions, particularly on high-uncertainty inputs. VGGT-Ω reports related blocky artifacts for all-MLP depth decoding in uncertain regions [17, Section 3.1.3]. We therefore retain the standard convolutional head for local point prediction. It reads the final decoder representation, without additional multi-layer feature fusion, to keep the design simple.

sections.title: 6.9 Surface Structure Refinement with 3D Sparse Convolution
sections.content: Following MoGe3 [7], we include 3D sparse-convolutional refinement stage that aggregates over geometric neighborhoods, reducing mixing between image-adjacent but depth-separated surfaces. In qualitative zero-shot tests, we apply the pretrained MoGe3 refiner to point clouds predicted by the convolutional head, replacing its image-derived conditioning features with zeros or random noise. In the examples shown in Figure 11, both settings yield more coherent surfaces and reduce distortions in thin structures near depth discontinuities. Despite these structural improvements, zero and random image conditioning increase mean normalized XYZ L1 error by 8.77% and 7.47%, respectively, relative to the coarse prediction in our diagnostic. We therefore condition our refiner on projected geometry-decoder features to guide structural corrections toward image-supported surface locations. 18 Figure 11: Surface refinement without informative image conditioning. From left to right: convolutional-head output, and pretrained-refiner results with image-derived conditioning features replaced by zeros or random noise, respectively. Both settings improve local structure while increasing point-placement error. Each comparison pairs an overview with close-up of the blueboxed thin structure.

sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.content: Cameraobject motion ambiguity. Although foreground-suppressed pseudo-labeling (Section 4.4) reduces reliance on dynamic foreground cues, π4 can still interpret moving foreground as stationary when the static background is weakly textured or the foreground is visually dominant. In these cases, the model confounds camera motion with object motion, yielding reconstruction that is inconsistent with the static background. Resolving this ambiguity requires scene and motion understanding beyond local texture correspondences. Sensitivity to distance from the coordinate origin. We observe larger camera-position errors for cameras farther from the reconstruction origin than for those near it. This suggests that pose accuracy may be sensitive to the coordinate representation and the numerical scale of absolute translations. Understanding this dependence and reducing sensitivity to the choice of coordinate origin and translation magnitude remain open problems. Accuracy and long-sequence generalization. π4 does not consistently match the accuracy of traditional geometric optimization methods, particularly when inference sequences are longer than those seen during training. Maintaining globally consistent camera trajectories and reconstructions under such sequence-length extrapolation remains challenging. Improving long-sequence generalization and closing the accuracy gap to optimization-based methods are important directions for future work.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We have presented π4, unified foundation model for 4D scene perception from diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations. With shared backbone and approximately 0.5B parameters, it combines dense geometry, camera pose, and metric-scale estimation with 2D/3D point tracking and movingobject segmentation. By predicting image-space correspondences conditioned on geometry and lifting them into the reconstructed 3D scene, π4 unifies geometry and motion in single forward pass. Across diverse benchmarks, π4 achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation and competitive performance in singleand multiview 2D/3D tracking and moving-object segmentation. It generalizes to diverse in-the-wild observations, producing coherent joint reconstructions and tracks from thousands of input images in large-scale scenes. Together with our data and training recipe and empirical studies of key design choices, these results mark step towards unified 4D scene perception.
